title.narrative: Making Cities and Human Settlements Safer after COVID-19: Strengthening Awareness of Safer Cities Tools applying a Human Security Framework

description.narrative: The COVID-19 pandemic casts a harsh and unforgiving light on - and accelerates - inequalities and social distress in urban environments across the globe. The pandemic has brought the attention of policy-makers and citizens to the way peoples’ lives and wellbeing are affected by a wide range of interconnected factors; also, to the fact that vulnerability, risks and threats are experienced very differently across gender, age, race and socio-economic divides. Covid-19 has not been an ‘equaliser’, but a shock to existing city-systems and infrastructures. It has amplified pre-existing inequalities and accelerated socio-economic processes that accentuate and generate vulnerabilities and multidimensional threats to people’s lives, livelihoods and fundamental rights. Among others, the pandemic has aggravated a crisis in the delivery of public safety. National and local government responses have placed heavy responsibility on security services. Many cities have fallen back into old emergency paradigms, abandoning lessons learned about the importance of systemic and collaborative approaches. This emergency approach has catalyzed further systemic vulnerabilities. Yet, the pandemic opens an opportunity to raise local and global awareness of the importance of developing safety and security strategies that are not only human-centred but comprehensive, context-specific and prevention-oriented and that promote integrated solutions ensuring greater coherence and stronger impact. Although the long term impact of the pandemic and its consequential shifts to local behaviours and patterns will not be understood for some time, it is crucial that local authorities are able to appraise their existing safety tools in light of the immediate effects of the pandemic on people’s safety in order to address people’s needs more effectively. Such endeavor requires a comprehensive approach to urban safety that uses the 7 dimensions of human security as guiding analytical framework to interrogate changes in social, economic, environmental, political, and mental ecologies of cities and urban communities, through a participatory and people-centred perspective. The common understanding of human security adopted by General Assembly resolution 66/290 has given rise to more tangible and sustainable results that comprehensively address the root causes behind current and emerging challenges on safety and security at the local level; helping to identify priorities based on the actual needs, vulnerabilities and capacities of Governments and people; and advance solutions that strengthen the protection and empowerment of all peoples and communities. The combination of these elements help bolster actions taken by the United Nations, Governments and other actors to build resilience, prevent crises and support people’s aspirations to be free from fear, want and indignity. In this light, UN-HABITAT and its Safer Cities Programme has been spearheading the urban safety approach in developing countries, through city projects and normative work at global and regional level. Initiated in 1996 to provide technical assistance to cities in order to strengthen their capacity to formulate and implement integrated local crime prevention strategies, the Programme promotes the implementation of the New Urban Agenda, which acknowledges the responsibility of local authorities in crime and violence prevention and is in line with the UN systemwide Guidelines on Safer Cities and Human Settlements. At the local level, the Programme provides direct support to local actors formulating and implementing local crime and violence prevention strategies. In the past years, the increasing mobilisation of local resources in support of crime and violence prevention and improved local partnerships on this issue led to total of 87 municipalities having adopted the Safer Cities approach, and growing unmet demand. At the global level, the Programme undertakes advocacy on local crime and violence prevention and enhancement of urban safety, policy development on human settlements and on the governance dimensions of a human-centred urban safety and security approach, documents and analyses experiences, and develops and disseminates tools for local governments and other actors. Among key outputs are an integrated set of tools and resources on urban safety, policy documents on key issues such as building safety through slum upgrading, gender violence, youth at risk and the role of the police in urban governance, regional strategies on youth at risk in Africa and Latin America, and an overall increased recognition of the key role of urban safety and security in sustainable urban development promoting inclusive cities.
